KP24 Combining Classifiers: Product, Sum, Majority Vote and the Bayesian View

Level: undergraduate, year 3

Pattern Recognition | Chapter 4, §4.21

Slides: read and download

Learning objectives

  • Explain the value of combining classifiers (complementary information) and write the product and sum rules with their KL derivations.
  • Explain the majority-vote formula, why independence is an illusion and the three ways to create diversity.
  • Explain the one-vote veto of the product rule and the Bayesian view, and know that no rule is always best.

KP24 Combining Classifiers: Product, Sum, Majority Vote and the Bayesian View

One-sentence summary: Even the best classifier errs on samples that others get right; complementary information is the whole value of combining. But combining does not guarantee a gain and there is no panacea.

1. Complementary information

Plain explanation: What is there to gain by combining classifiers?

Example (designed here): logistic, a depth-4 tree and 3-NN on noisy half-moons (100 training points per class, 2000 new points in all): 85.2%, 82.6% and 87.8% on new points. The best, 3-NN, is wrong on 12.2%, and for 60% of those at least one other classifier is right. But the vote of the three gets only 86.2%, below the 87.8% of 3-NN; complementary information must be mined to be worth anything.

Figure lec05-kp24-comp: the accuracies of three classifiers and the share of complementary errors.

2. The product rule

KL distance D=∑iPln⁡(P/Pj)D=\sum_iP\ln(P/P_j)D=∑i​Pln(P/Pj​): how far apart two probability distributions are; asymmetric, so strictly not a distance. The product rule (formal definition): minimizing 1L∑jDj\tfrac1L\sum_jD_jL1​∑j​Dj​ gives

P(ωi∣x)=1C∏j=1LPj(ωi∣x)1/L, P(\omega_i|x)=\frac1C\prod_{j=1}^{L}P_j(\omega_i|x)^{1/L}, P(ωi​∣x)=C1​j=1∏L​Pj​(ωi​∣x)1/L,

and the class with the largest product is chosen. Example: two classes, three classifiers (0.8,0.2)(0.8,0.2)(0.8,0.2), (0.6,0.4)(0.6,0.4)(0.6,0.4), (0.7,0.3)(0.7,0.3)(0.7,0.3): products 0.336 against 0.024, so ω1\omega_1ω1​.

Figure lec05-kp24-prod: the product rule and the example.

3. The sum rule

Sum rule: swap the two arguments of DjD_jDj​ (PjP_jPj​ first) and the optimum is P(ωi∣x)=1L∑jPj(ωi∣x)P(\omega_i|x)=\tfrac1L\sum_jP_j(\omega_i|x)P(ωi​∣x)=L1​∑j​Pj​(ωi​∣x), the arithmetic mean. For the same three classifiers: means 0.70 against 0.30, also ω1\omega_1ω1​. Each rule has a rigorous information-theoretic origin; there is no theoretical preference, and in practice the product is clean but fragile when an output is near zero, and in practice the sum is often safer (source [Mill 99]).

Figure lec05-kp24-sum: the sum rule and the example.

4. The veto

Example (designed here): five classifiers give the correct class ω1\omega_1ω1​ the values 0.7, 0.7, 0.7, 0.7, 0.001 (the rest to ω2\omega_2ω2​). The product gives ω1\omega_1ω1​ 0.00024 against ω2\omega_2ω2​ 0.00809, wrong; the sum 0.5602 against 0.4398, right; the vote is 4 to 1, right. A single near-zero factor drags the whole product to zero, a one-vote veto.

Figure lec05-kp24-veto: the outputs of five classifiers and the result of three rules.

5. Majority vote

Majority vote: decide only if at least lcl_clc​ classifiers agree (lc=L+12l_c=\tfrac{L+1}2lc​=2L+1​ for odd LLL); otherwise reject. For independent decisions with equal accuracy ppp,

Pc(L)=∑m=lcL(Lm)pm(1−p)L−m. P_c(L)=\sum_{m=l_c}^{L}\binom Lm p^m(1-p)^{L-m}. Pc​(L)=m=lc​∑L​(mL​)pm(1−p)L−m.

p=0.6p=0.6p=0.6: L=3L=3L=3: 0.648, L=11L=11L=11: 0.754, L=51L=51L=51: 0.927; p=0.55p=0.55p=0.55: L=51L=51L=51: 0.764; p=0.45p=0.45p=0.45: L=51L=51L=51: 0.236; p=0.5p=0.5p=0.5 stays 0.5.

Figure lec05-kp24-vote: Pc(L)P_c(L)Pc​(L) against LLL.

6. The independence illusion

Example (designed here): the half-moon data of KP23, 20 training sets, 25 bagged trees each, 2000 new points. A single tree gets 83.8% on average; the independence formula Pc(25,p)P_c(25,p)Pc​(25,p) gives 99.99%; the real majority vote 87.7%; the share of member decisions differing from the majority is V=0.095V=0.095V=0.095. The trees are trained on resamples of the same data, so their mistakes are strongly shared. Common misconception: as long as every classifier beats guessing the vote tends to 100%; this relies on independence, which fails in practice and the more so the larger LLL (source).

Figure lec05-kp24-indep: a single tree, the independence formula and the real vote.

7. Creating diversity

Diversity: how much the members' decisions differ; one measure is VVV, the share of member decisions that differ from the majority. Three ways (source): the same feature space with different data points (bootstrap, most effective for unstable trees); different classifier types; different feature subspaces. Experiment (designed here, 10-D, 150 points, 15 runs): one tree 71.2%; 11 bootstrap trees 77.9±2.1% (V=0.197V=0.197V=0.197); 11 random-subset trees 75.9±2.3% (0.241); 5 classifiers 82.1±1.2% (0.114). The ensemble with the largest VVV is not the most accurate, and the 5 classifiers include logistic regression, which happens to suit this data, so we cannot conclude that different classifiers are always better.

Figure lec05-kp24-div: the vote accuracy and VVV of three ensemble types.

8. The Bayesian view and how to remember

Assuming independent xjx_jxj​ gives max⁡kP(ωk)1−L∏jP(ωk∣xj)\max_kP(\omega_k)^{1-L}\prod_jP(\omega_k|x_j)maxk​P(ωk​)1−L∏j​P(ωk​∣xj​): the product rule again, but very sensitive to errors in the posterior estimates; the sum tolerates errors better and often beats the product in practice (source [Kitt 98]). The source's handwritten-digit experiments: no rule is always best; in some cases the combination is worse than the best single classifier; combining one classifier on different feature sets works best (our random subsets on page 7 did worst). Page 1 agrees: the vote gets 86.2%, below 87.8%. To remember: the sum and the majority vote are the most used; there is no panacea theorem.

Figure lec05-kp24-bayes: the Bayesian view and the trade-offs of the three rules.

Extension: the median, practice and worked solution

The median (designed here): five classifiers give ω1\omega_1ω1​: 0.80, 0.85, 0.75, 0.01, 0.01. The sum gives 0.484 against 0.516, wrong; the product 5.1×10−55.1\times10^{-5}5.1×10−5 against 7.4×10−37.4\times10^{-3}7.4×10−3, wrong; the median 0.75 against 0.25, right. With outlying outputs the sum is pulled away while the median holds; the source also mentions max, min and median, motivated by the chain product ≤ min ≤ mean ≤ max.

Figure lec05-kp24-median: the three rules with two extreme outputs.
